question: On 16 February 2024, a Chinese-Hungarian law enforcement summit was held in Budapest, where China’s Minister of Public Security, Wang Xiaohong, and the Hungarian Interior Minister, Sándor Pintér, signed agreements on strengthening law enforcement cooperation and joint patrols.1 Earlier, China concluded a similar agreement with Serbia, an EU candidate country, where Chinese police officers are now patrolling areas popular with Chinese businesses or tourists.2 1.
Has the Hungarian Government informed the Commission about this cooperation and, if so, can the Commission provide details?

Does the Commission agree that these planned Chinese-Hungarian law enforcement cooperation and joint patrols in EU territory pose an enormous threat to democracy, public security and EU law enforcement cooperation?
Will the Commission start an infringement procedure against the Hungarian Government?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2024) The Commission’s services acquired knowledge of two Memoranda of Understanding signed between Hungary and China concerning law enforcement cooperation, in the context of the recent Schengen evaluation carried out in Hungary.

At the Commission’s request, Hungary has communicated the two Memoranda of Understanding, while specifying that the joint patrols of Chinese and Hungarian police officers referred to in these instruments are not, for the time being, in operation.

While Member States are responsible for the maintenance of law and order on their territory, police cooperation needs to be exercised in line with the principle of sincere cooperation, in full respect of applicable EU law and fundamental rights.

On 24 July 2024, Commissioner for Home Affairs wrote to Hungary’s Interior Minister, underlying that the envisaged law enforcement cooperation of Hungary with China raises questions in relation to its compliance with EU law notably as regards police cooperation and the protection of personal data.

She has also expressed concerns about the impact such cooperation could have on the level of cooperation and mutual trust between Member States in police cooperation, which risks undermining the cohesion necessary for the protection of the Schengen area.

When EU law applies, the Commission oversees its respect by Member States and makes use of a variety of tools to monitor, promote and enforce its correct application, including infringement proceedings1.

The Commission is now assessing the compliance of the two Memoranda of Understanding with EU law and has requested the Hungarian authorities to provide the necessary information on the purpose and scope of these instruments, and to explain how, in their view, they could be consistent with Hungary’s obligations under EU law.
Depending on the result of its assessment, the Commission will decide on possible next steps and not hesitate to exercise as necessary its role as guardian of the Treaties.
